Notes: 586 BCE (Nebuchadnezzar's 18th year): Jeremiah 52:29 - 832 persons taken into exile from Jerusalem (deportation after the destruction of the First Temple; deportees were brought to Babylonia, not counted as residents of the city of Babylon). Jeremiah 52:28-30 gives 3,023 Judeans exiled in the 7th year (597 BCE), 832 in the 18th and 745 in the 23rd year, 4,600 in all - deportation figures for all of Babylonia, so Population blank. Year Established -597 = deportation of King Jehoiachin, the Judean elite and craftsmen to Babylon in 597 BCE (Jeremiah 52:28; 2 Kings 24:15), confirmed by oil-ration lists from the South Palace of Babylon dated 591 BCE naming Jehoiachin, his five sons and other Judeans (see Alstola rows).

582/581 BCE (Nebuchadnezzar's 23rd year): Jeremiah 52:30 - Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, took into exile 745 Judeans (third deportation; total of the three deportations 4,600). Deportation count for Babylonia as a whole, not a count of Jews resident in the city of Babylon; Population blank.

c. 561 BCE (accession year of Amel-Marduk/Evil-merodach, 562/561 BCE; 37th year of the exile): 2 Kings 25:27-30 - the deposed King Jehoiachin of Judah released from prison in Babylon, given a seat 'above the other seats of the kings who were with him in Babylon' and a regular royal allowance for life. Literary attestation of the exiled Judean royal household living in the city of Babylon (a small court group; no number). Alstola (2017) regards the amnesty account as literary rather than a historical record.

537 BCE (19-IV-2 Cyrus): cuneiform receipt of a rental payment concerning a house in Babylon owned by a man with a Yahwistic name, Ia-'-u-[...] (text Cyr 43, written in Babylon), per T. Alstola, Judeans in Babylonia (Leiden PhD 2017), ch. 6.4. A Judean property owner in the city of Babylon early in the Persian period; individual attestation, no community size given.

518 BCE (4th year of Darius I): promissory note B5 (CUSAS 28) for over five minas of silver and five sheep, written in Babylon, records Ahiqam son of Rapa-Yama of the Judean village of Yahudu with Judean debtor and witnesses (Yahwistic names) transacting in Babylon; Alstola (2017, ch. 4) concludes this group 'had travelled from the countryside to Babylon'. Evidence of Judean commercial activity in the capital (Ahiqam later ran a beer-brewing and retail business in Babylon), but these individuals were visitors, not residents; Population blank.

507 BCE (3-X-14 Darius I; unpublished tablet BM 26553 written in Babylon): members of prominent Babylonian prebendary families paid a tax of 15 kurru of barley to a Judean sepiru (official), son of Zakar-Yama, apparently a subordinate of the rab kasiri (royal treasury official) - 'a government official of some importance' (Alstola 2017, ch. 6.1). Individual Judean official active in Babylon.

c. 506 BCE (5-VII-16(?) Darius I; the copy may read year 19 = 503 BCE): inheritance division (CUSAS 28 C45 || A2) of Ahiqam's beer-brewing business assets in Babylon (vats and two slaves) among his sons. Alstola (2017, ch. 4) notes 'the great number of Judean witnesses in Babylon sheds some light on the Judean community in the capital' and, since none appear elsewhere in the Yahudu corpus, 'it is unlikely that they all travelled from Yahudu to Babylon' - i.e. evidence of a resident Judean community in the city of Babylon in the late 6th c. BCE; size not given.

486 BCE (24-VI-36 Darius I; BM 74554, ed. Stolper 1989, written in Babylon): Gadal-Yama son of Banna-Ea, a Judean, served as sepiru bel temi (high administrative official) under the governor of Babylon and Across-the-River and authorised the collection of a tax of 14 kurru of barley - 'a unique example of a Judean working in the provincial administration in Babylonia' (Alstola 2017, ch. 6.1). Individual Judean official in Babylon.

458 BCE (7th year of Artaxerxes I): Ezra 7:6-9 - Ezra the scribe 'came up from Babylonia' (Hebrew mi-Bavel, which can denote either the city of Babylon or the land) to Jerusalem with priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers and temple servants. Literary attestation of a Judean community 'in Babylon' in the Persian period; the departing group's size is not given in these verses; Population blank.

Persian period (539-332 BCE; midpoint -435): Encyclopaedia Judaica ('Babylonia') states that after the Achaemenid return edict 'there is virtually no specific evidence concerning the status of the Jewish community of Babylon', but that such a community remained, as shown by its mention as the home of Ezra and its existence in post-Achaemenid times. The same article notes that under the Seleucids Babylon declined and that Antiochus I transferred a considerable Semitic population from Babylon to Seleucia in 275 BCE (Jews not specified). Continuity of presence; no figure.

c. 210 BCE: letter of Antiochus III (Josephus, Antiquities 12.149 = 12.3.4) ordering the removal of 'two thousand families of Jews, with their effects, out of Mesopotamia and Babylon' to fortresses in Lydia and Phrygia (~10,000 persons at 5 per family). 'Babylon' here denotes the region of Babylonia together with Mesopotamia, and the figure counts transferred settlers, not residents of the city; Population blank. Date c. 210 BCE per Encyclopaedia Judaica.

c. 38-36 BCE: Josephus, Antiquities 15.2.2 (15.14) - the Parthian king Phraates (IV, accession c. 38/37 BCE) released the captive former high priest Hyrcanus II 'and gave him a habitation at Babylon, where there were Jews in great numbers', who honoured him as high priest and king. Ancient literary attestation of a large Jewish population, no number. Whiston's footnote: 'The city here called Babylon by Josephus, seems to be one which was built by some of the Seleucidae upon the Tigris... not far from Seleucia', i.e. possibly not old Babylon on the Euphrates (ancient Babylon was largely deserted by this time).

c. 37 BCE: Josephus, Antiquities 15.2.4 (15.22) - Herod 'sent for an obscure priest out of Babylon, whose name was Ananelus' (Hananel) and made him high priest; 15.3.1 (15.39) calls him one of the Jews 'carried captive beyond the Euphrates'. Individual Jew from Babylon (city or region uncertain).

c. 35 CE (after the fall of Anilaeus's party; the Anilaeus-Asinaeus episode in Babylonia is dated c. 20-35 CE): Josephus, Antiquities 18.371-372 - 'the Babylonians attacked the Jews', with whom they 'were almost always at variance, by reason of the contrariety of their laws'; the Jews, 'neither able to fight them, nor bearing to live with them, ... went to Seleucia'. Persecution and emigration of the Jews of Babylon(ia) to Seleucia on the Tigris. Population blank (not 0): the text does not say that no Jews remained; scholars (Goodblatt 1987) question Josephus's sequence.

c. 40 CE ('on the sixth year' after the flight to Seleucia): Josephus, Antiquities 18.373 - 'a pestilence came upon these at Babylon, which occasioned new removals of men's habitations out of that city'; the newcomers' arrival in Seleucia was followed by a massacre of the Jews there (Ant. 18.374-376; the casualty figure belongs to Seleucia, not Babylon). Further emigration of Jews from the city of Babylon; Population blank (no statement that none remained).

c. 40 CE (Philo's Embassy to Gaius, written after 41 CE): Philo, Legatio 216 - Gaius knew that 'Babylon and many others of the satrapies of the east were occupied by the Jews'; Legatio 282 - 'Babylon, and all the satrapies around, which have any advantages whatever of soil or climate, have Jews settled in them'. Ancient literary attestation of a substantial Jewish population in Babylon (city or Babylonia) in the early 1st c. CE; no number.
